editorial.headline: Tourism by Inland Water: River and Lake Passenger Transport in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers tourist passenger journeys on inland waterways, open to PMA nationally and not blocked by Bali’s PMA moratorium.
editorial.body:
This activity is about carrying passengers for tourism across Indonesia’s inland waters: rivers, canals, lakes, swamps and other inland waterways. Its scope is deliberately broader than a single type of excursion or customer. It can serve an individual traveller, an organised group, a family, or a social purpose, provided the journey is tourist passenger transport on those waters. The organising idea is not the destination alone, but the movement of visitors by inland water.

A business registering this activity is therefore placing tourist passenger transport at the centre of its operation. The record opens it to Menengah and Besar scales, making scale an explicit part of the registration picture rather than an afterthought. That matters because the activity is defined by both its tourism purpose and its setting: inland waterways, not a generic transport category. The wording also accommodates the different ways tourism is experienced—privately, collectively, with family, or through social activity—without narrowing the activity to only one kind of passenger.

Nationally, the PMA position is straightforward. The status is TERBUKA and the maximum foreign ownership is 100%. In practical terms, the national record does not impose a foreign-ownership ceiling below full ownership for this activity. That is the national starting point: tourist passenger transport on rivers, canals, lakes, swamps and other inland waters is open for PMA registration at the stated scales.

Bali requires its own reading, because the province permanently blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk activities. This activity is not in that blocked position. Its Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the record says that at Besar scale its OSS risk is Medium-High or High; it is therefore not blocked by the moratorium. The result is clear: for PMA registration, this activity remains open in Bali rather than being shut out by the provincial moratorium. A founder should keep the national 100% ceiling and Bali’s non-blocked status in view together, without mistaking the province’s general moratorium for a prohibition on this activity.
